title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns give Democrats a clear lesson for deep-red states. In places where the party label hurts, the stronger path is often a local independent with a focused economic message.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.
Nebraska is not a normal Democratic target. Republicans dominate the state. The Democratic brand carries a heavy cost. A standard Democratic nominee starts behind before the campaign begins.

Osborn found a different lane. He ran as an independent. He leaned on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He made the race about work, wages, political insiders, and corporate power.

That mattered in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but he held the race close by Nebraska standards. Fischer won by about six points. In a state where Republicans usually win federal races by much more, that result proved something important.
The lesson was simple. Some voters who reject national Democrats will still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economic pressure.
This matters for Democratic strategy. In deep-red states, the goal should not always be to build the strongest Democratic nominee. Your goal should be to build the strongest anti-Republican race.

Those are different goals. A Democrat on the ballot gives loyal party voters a clear choice. An independent like Osborn gives unhappy Republicans, union households, rural voters, and nonpartisan voters more space to cross over.

The 2026 race sharpens this strategy. Osborn is running against Republican Senator Pete Ricketts. Ricketts is wealthy, well known, and tied closely to Nebraska Republican politics. Osborn has a clear contrast. Worker against billionaire. Outsider against insider. Local labor figure against political dynasty.
That contrast is the core of his campaign. If the race centers on national party control, Ricketts benefits. If the race centers on class, work, and independence, Osborn gains room.

Nebraska Democrats appear to understand this. Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary, then said she would withdraw and support Osborn. That move reduces the risk of a split anti-Ricketts vote. It also keeps Osborn from running a three-way race where Republicans need only hold their base.
This is the part Democrats should study. In a deep-red state, stepping aside is sometimes more strategic than staying on the ballot. Party pride does not win races. Vote math wins races.

The Osborn model does not work everywhere. You need a candidate with local credibility. You need a message voters believe. You need a state where voters have some history of ticket splitting or independent streaks. You also need national Democrats to stay disciplined.

That last part is key. If national Democrats flood the race and turn Osborn into a party project, they weaken his brand. His strength comes from distance. Distance from Washington. Distance from party leaders. Distance from the normal partisan script.

That does not mean Democrats should do nothing. They should clear the field when useful. They should avoid attacking the independent. Donors who want a larger Senate map should help without taking over the campaign. State parties should focus on turnout, ballot access, and voter education.

For your forecast model, Osborn creates a special case. Nebraska is still red. Ricketts starts with real advantages. Republican voters are more likely to return home as Election Day gets closer. Outside groups will try to define Osborn as a Democrat.

But the race deserves attention because Osborn changes the normal assumptions. He expands the map without pretending Nebraska has become blue. He gives Democrats and anti-Ricketts voters a path based on candidate fit, not party strength.

That is why his 2026 campaign matters. A win would reshape Senate strategy. A close loss would still give Democrats useful evidence. The old plan of running standard nominees in deep-red states often produces predictable losses. Osborn offers a better test.
Your takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.

title: Paths for Democratic Control
dek: Democrats' majority path starts with holding Michigan and flipping North Carolina and Maine, then runs through Ohio, Texas, or Alaska.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: In 2026, Democrats start at a disadvantage: more than twenty of the thirty-five seats up for election are in states Trump carried by more than five points. Still, Trump's weak approval and Democratic overperformance in 2025 and early 2026 elections give the party a narrow Senate path.

In almost any Democratic majority scenario, North Carolina and Maine have to flip. The current forecast gives Maine about a 71% chance of electing a Democrat and North Carolina an over 88% chance of electing former Gov. Roy Cooper, making those two races the foundation of the Democratic path.

If Democrats flip North Carolina and Maine, Michigan becomes vital to hold. The state has a close three-way Democratic Primary, and the eventual nominee is likely to face Mike Rogers in a tough election. Despite what looks to be a tough election season for Michigan, the model currently gives Democrats roughly a 70% chance of holding the seat.

That would leave Democrats needing two more flips, most likely from Ohio, Texas, and Alaska. Ohio has the strongest chance out of the three to flip for Democrats, but the forecast shows it as close, with only a 55% of flipping. Texas and Alaska are harder, but either could flip if the national environment keeps moving toward Democrats.
